elements.id-string-3: The clustering algorithm plays a crucial role in speaker diarization systems.
elements.id-string-4: However, traditional clustering algorithms suffer from the complex distribution of speaker embeddings and lack of digging potential relationships between speakers in a session.
elements.id-string-5: We propose a novel graph-based clustering approach called Community Detection Graph Convolutional Network (CDGCN) to improve the performance of the speaker diarization system.
elements.id-string-6: The CDGCN-based clustering method consists of graph generation, sub-graph detection, and Graph-based Overlapped Speech Detection (Graph-OSD).
elements.id-string-7: Firstly, the graph generation refines the local linkages among speech segments.
elements.id-string-8: Secondly the sub-graph detection finds the optimal global partition of the speaker graph.
elements.id-string-9: Finally, we view speaker clustering for overlap-aware speaker diarization as an overlapped community detection task and design a Graph-OSD component to output overlap-aware labels.
elements.id-string-10: By capturing local and global information, the speaker diarization system with CDGCN clustering outperforms the traditional Clustering-based Speaker Diarization (CSD) systems on the DIHARD III corpus.

elements.id-string-14: Speaker diarization is a problem of grouping speech segments in
elements.id-string-15: an audio recording according to the speakers’ identities.
elements.id-string-16: We have witnessed the rising popularity of speaker diarization over recent years for its significant applications of minutes of meetings, multi-speaker transcription, pre-processing for automatic speech recognition (ASR) \cite{boeddeker2018front}\cite{medennikov2020stc}, and so on.
elements.id-string-17: As the deployments for scenarios have grown in complexity, speaker diarization systems confront many difficulties, such as the unknown number of speakers and handling the overlapped speech.

elements.id-string-19: Clustering-based approaches are widely used in speaker diarization because it allows for flexible and scalable speaker modeling using various techniques \cite{shum2013unsupervised}\cite{sell2014speaker}\cite{ning2006spectral}.
elements.id-string-20: There are three modules in clustering-based Speaker Diarization (CSD) systems: speaker embedding extractor, clustering module, and post-processing module.
elements.id-string-21: Typically, the clustering modules in CSD systems utilize conventional clustering algorithms, such as Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (AHC) \cite{sell2016priors}\cite{xiao2021microsoft}, Spectral Clustering (SC) \cite{wang22ha_interspeech}\cite{lin2020self}\cite{lin19_interspeech} and K-means\cite{wang2018speaker}, to perform speaker embeddings clustering.
elements.id-string-22: However, traditional conventional clustering algorithms suffer from complicated distribution of speaker embeddings \cite{shi2000normalized} and is sensitive to hyper-parameter.
elements.id-string-23: For example, SC assumes the sizes of clusters are relatively balanced, while K-means assumes the clusters are spherical.
elements.id-string-24: Moreover, the performance of AHC is affected by the threshold sensitively.
elements.id-string-25: These assumptions limit the speaker clustering performance and degrade the diarization quality.
elements.id-string-26: The distribution of speakers is hard to be modeled with Euclidean structures, because of the complex interrelation among speakers.
elements.id-string-27: Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) \cite{welling2016semi} is proposed to handle the data of non-Euclidean structure.
elements.id-string-28: Many GCN-based clustering methods are recently proposed for large-scale embeddings clustering instead of relying on hand-crafted criteria.
elements.id-string-29: Tong et al. \cite{tong2022graph} adopted Detection Segmentation Graph Convolutional Network (DSGCN) for semi-supervised speaker recognition.
elements.id-string-30: Wang et al. \cite{wang2020speaker} used a GCN to refine speaker embeddings for affinity matrix on speaker diarization system.
elements.id-string-31: Inspired by these works, we proposed a new GCN-based clustering approach with community detection for speaker diarization named Community Detection Graph Convolutional Network (CDGCN).
elements.id-string-32: We regard the clustering of speaker embeddings as a speaker graph generation and sub-graph detection task.
elements.id-string-33: The key idea is to build a refined speaker graph for segment embeddings and globally partition speaker graph to assign speaker labels for segments.
elements.id-string-34: The CDGCN-based clustering method also can assign multi-labels for each node to handle overlapped speech.

elements.id-string-74: The basic concept of the CDGCN is to estimate the topological connection of speech segments and use a community detection algorithm to find the optimal partitions.
elements.id-string-75: CDGCN-based clustering method contains graph generation, sub-graphs detection, and graph-based overlapped speech detection (Graph-OSD).
elements.id-string-76: Each component of CDGCN will be described as follows.
elements.id-string-78: The input of clustering module is a raw graph ${\mathcal{G}}=(\mathcal{V},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{E})}$, where nodes $\mathcal{V}=\{{v}_{1}, {v}_{2},...,{v}_{N}\} \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ represent speech segments, edges $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{E}} = \{\boldsymbol{e}_{1},\boldsymbol{e}_{2},...,\boldsymbol{e}_{N}\} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ are cosine similarity scores between pairs of embeddings and $N$ is the number of segments.
elements.id-string-79: The raw graph is a complex full-connected graph which is vulnerable to noise.
elements.id-string-80: In order to tackle this problem, we design a graph generation to refine interrelations between speech segments according to local context information.
elements.id-string-81: Firstly, we adopt the $K$-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm to create sub-graphs for each node.
elements.id-string-82: The sub-graph $\mathcal{G}_{n}=(\mathcal{V}_{n},\mathcal{E}_{n})$ is built for $n$-th pivot node, where $\mathcal{V}_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ is the top-$K$ nearest neighbor of pivot node and $\mathcal{E}_{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ denotes the similarity among $n$-th pivot node and its neighbors.
elements.id-string-83: For example, as shown in Figure \ref{fig:cdgcn} (a), let $K$ and the nodes number $N$ be 6 and 12 respectively.
elements.id-string-84: The raw speaker sub-graphs $\mathcal{G}_{n}$ are fed into GCN model mentioned in Section \ref{sec:Review} and the refined sub-graphs $\mathcal{\hat{G}}_{n}=(\mathcal{V}_{n},\mathcal{\hat{E}}_{n})$ are predicted, where $\mathcal{\hat{E}}_{n}=\{\hat{e}_{n}^{1},\hat{e}_{n}^{2},...,\hat{e}_{n}^{K}\}\in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ are predicted edges and $\hat{e}_{n}^{K}$ indicates the probability that pivot node and $k$-th node belong to the same cluster.

elements.id-string-95: Community detection aims to group nodes with an optimization quality function.

elements.id-string-104: The Leiden community detection consists of the following phases:
elements.id-string-105: (1) \textbf{Initial partition}: The Leiden algorithm assigns each node to a singleton community.
elements.id-string-106: (2) \textbf{Nodes Local moving}: The individual node is moved from one community to another to find a better partition $P$ with higher Q.
elements.id-string-107: (3) \textbf{Partition refinement}: In the refinement phase, the refined partition $P_{refined}$ is initially set to a singleton partition.
elements.id-string-108: And then, the nodes in each community are merged locally to refine partition $P_{refined}$.
elements.id-string-109: After performing refinement, communities in $P$ may be split into subcommunities.
elements.id-string-110: (4) \textbf{Graph aggregation}: An aggregation graph is constructed based on $P_{refined}$.
elements.id-string-111: In this phase, the node belonging to the same community are merged into a new node.
elements.id-string-112: (5) \textbf{Iteration}: Phases 2-4 are repeated until no further improvements of quality function can be made.
elements.id-string-114: Overlapped speech handling is the critical processing of speaker diarization.

elements.id-string-117: The Graph-OSD is a two-stage model to handle overlapped speech and assume there are at most two speakers at once.

elements.id-string-198: This paper proposes a novel speaker clustering method based on the speaker topological graph for speaker diarization.
elements.id-string-199: We aim to give consideration to both local and global information when clustering.
elements.id-string-200: The proposed CDGCN-based clustering approach include graph generation, sub-graphs detection, and Graph-OSD.
elements.id-string-201: The local linkage between speech segments is inferred by a GCN model, while the Leiden community detection algorithm is applied to find the global partition of the speaker graph.
elements.id-string-202: To further improve the performance of our speaker diarization system, we also proposed a Graph-OSD component to handle overlapped speech for speaker diarization.
elements.id-string-203: Experimental results demonstrated that CDGCN based speaker diarization system outperformed conventional CSD systems in the DIHARD III corpus.
